summary:
AURA is a health monitoring system for astronauts. A wristband with an ESP32 measures heart rate, blood oxygen, movement and cabin air (temperature, humidity, pressure and carbon monoxide). A server interprets the data instantly with predefined rules and tells the astronaut, in plain language, what happened, why it matters and what to do.

Today most medical interpretation happens on Earth; on missions to the Moon or Mars, communication delays make that too slow. AURA brings body, air and reported symptoms together and turns each alert into action without relying on Earth. A doctor on Earth receives the same data with a delay, plus trend graphs and a log.

Some rules combine sensors: a high heart rate while moving is exercise, not an alarm. Carbon monoxide triggers an alert on its own, because a pulse oximeter cannot tell CO-bound from oxygenated hemoglobin and keeps reading 98% during poisoning.

The PWA shows a 3D particle body whose zones (mind, oxygen, cabin air, heart, body) change color with each alert. It includes sensor preflight, impact detection with a 30-second "Are you OK?" prompt, symptom logging, signal-loss alerts and a scenario simulator.

Stack: ESP32 + PlatformIO, Node.js, Express, Socket.IO, Prisma, PostgreSQL, React, Vite and three.js. Prototype, not a medical device: thresholds are not clinical and critical scenarios were validated in simulation.
details:
AURA (Astronaut Unified Readiness Assistant) is an onboard health monitor that lets an astronaut understand and act on their own health without waiting for Earth.

How it works

A wrist-worn device built on an ESP32 measures pulse and blood oxygen (MAX30100, fingertip), motion and impacts (MPU6050), and the cabin air: temperature, humidity, pressure (AHT20 + BMP280) and a carbon monoxide index (MQ-7). Every ~2 seconds it sends the readings over HTTPS to a server, which validates them, stores them and runs a rule engine. When something goes wrong, the astronaut gets an alert in plain language with three parts: what happened, why it matters, and what to do now. Critical alerts are also evaluated on the device itself, with an OLED screen and a buzzer, so they work even with no network. A "Ground" view receives the same data with a deliberate delay to show that the crew acts first and Earth reviews later, as it would on a Mars mission.

What makes it different

- Body and cabin together. AURA alarms on carbon monoxide by itself, because a pulse oximeter confuses CO-bound hemoglobin with oxygen and keeps reading normal during poisoning. A system that only watches SpO2 would miss it.

- Context. A high pulse while moving is exercise and does not alert; the same pulse at rest, sustained above the astronaut's own baseline, is flagged as possible acute stress.

- Silence is not "all clear": if the device stops sending for 10 seconds, AURA raises a critical alert.

- After an impact it asks "Are you OK?" and escalates to the crew if there is no answer in 30 seconds.

- The interface is a 3D particle body with five zones (mind, blood oxygen, cabin air, heart, body) that shows status at a glance, designed for a stressed user who needs one clear next step.

Tools

Hardware: ESP32 DevKit V1, MAX30100, MPU6050, AHT20 + BMP280, MQ-7, SSD1306 OLED, active buzzer, MB102 power module; firmware in C++ with PlatformIO.

Software: TypeScript; Node.js with Express 5, Socket.IO, Zod and Prisma on PostgreSQL; a React + Vite + three.js progressive web app. A shared package holds the telemetry contract, the rule engine and a simulator, so real and simulated data follow exactly the same path.

What we considered

We designed for honesty about the data: all simulated data is labeled SIMULATED, the CO reading is a relative index (not calibrated ppm), and thresholds are initial engineering values informed by NASA crew health and cabin atmosphere standards, not clinical limits. AURA is a prototype, not a medical device. We also designed for a crew that cannot wait for Earth, for false alarms that erode trust, and for hardware that a student team can build and replicate cheaply.

Intended impact

Give astronauts on long missions early, understandable warnings about their body and their environment, so they can protect themselves first, while keeping the flight surgeon informed.
